Kirk's dik-dik (Madoqua kirkii) exhibits a remarkably low basal metabolic rate for an ungulate of its size, with respirometry trials on captive individuals at a core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] yielding an oxygen consumption of 2671 milliliters per hour [JOi = 2671 milliliters per hour]. This metabolic economy is thought to be an adaptation to the arid and semi-arid savannas of eastern and southwestern Africa, where the species must contend with high ambient temperatures and seasonally scarce forage. The measured value is considerably lower than that predicted by standard mammalian allometric equations for a 5 to 7 kilogram antelope, a disparity that aligns with the dik-dik's strategy of minimizing energy expenditure in a resource-limited environment. Such efficient physiology allows it to maintain a stable body temperature even during the hottest part of the day, when many other sympatric herbivores seek shade. This resting metabolic trait underscores the suite of adaptations that enable Kirk's dik-dik to thrive in dry, open habitats where water and high-quality browse are sporadically distributed.

Reproductive output in Kirk's dik-dik follows a pattern typical of small antelopes, with females producing a single calf per litter [N_R_i = single calf per litter] and giving birth to two litters each year [F_R_i = two litters each year]. This schedule, recorded in a captive population maintained at a constant ambient temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], represents the maximum achievable annual reproductive rate for the species and reflects a life-history strategy that balances high offspring investment with relatively rapid population turnover. Each calf is born at a wet weight of 600 grams [Wwb = 600 grams], a substantial neonate relative to maternal body mass, which facilitates a precocial development pattern allowing the fawn to follow the mother within days of parturition. The combination of modest litter size and multiple annual breeding events is characteristic of antelopes inhabiting unpredictable environments, where the ability to replace losses quickly confers a selective advantage. This reproductive rate positions Kirk's dik-dik at the fast end of the continuum among similarly sized bovids.

Size dimorphism is pronounced in Kirk's dik-dik, with adult females attaining an ultimate body mass of 7200 grams [Wwi = 7200 grams], whereas males reach a final mass of only 6400 grams [Wwi = 6400 grams]. This discrepancy is likely driven by the selective pressures of a monogamous mating system in which males invest heavily in territorial defense rather than in gaining mass. The smaller adult size of males permits greater agility in patrolling and defending fixed home ranges against conspecifics, a behavioral necessity in their patchy bushland habitat. In a comparative context, these asymptotic masses are notably lower than those of most other members of the subfamily Antilopinae, with the dik-dik's diminutive frame being one of its most distinctive features. The juvenile growth trajectory that culminates in these adult sizes is punctuated by the cessation of maternal provisioning, which occurs at a wet weight of 1780 grams [Wwx = 1780 grams] at weaning, a milestone that marks the transition to independent foraging and is critical for understanding the species' population dynamics.

The developmental chronology of Kirk's dik-dik under typical physiological conditions (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]) reveals a tightly orchestrated series of life-cycle events. Gestation in females lasts 172 days [tg = 172 days], a duration that is relatively short for a bovid of this size but consistent with the high reproductive turnover characteristic of the species at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. Following birth, maternal care extends through a nursing period of 71 days [tx = 71 days] until weaning is complete, after which the calf must subsist entirely on browse at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This sex-based divergence in maturation timing is commonly observed in polygynous or pair-bonding ungulates and may relate to the prolonged period required for males to achieve the body size and social status necessary for successful territory acquisition.

Maximum documented longevity in Kirk's dik-dik reaches approximately 6315 days [am = approximately 6315 days] under conditions approximating their natural body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], a lifespan that is comparatively long for a small antelope and likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates afforded by effective anti-predator behavior and a cryptic, thicket-dwelling lifestyle. This extended survival, recorded in both field studies of marked individuals and captive collections, allows for multiple reproductive seasons and contributes to stable population structure even when annual fecundity is constrained. In the context of the species' slow-paced metabolism and small body size, such a lifespan is all the more remarkable and illustrates how life-history traits covary across taxa. The interplay between this delayed senescence, the moderate gestation period, and the protracted sexual maturation of males paints a picture of a species finely tuned to the ecological realities of its fragmented savanna habitat.
